home.title: Leon knows everything you want
home.lead: Leon reads your team’s tools and answers in plain English. Every sentence links to the original. When nothing on record supports an answer, it says so.
home.assistantTitle: Give your AI assistant your team’s context.
home.assistantLead: Leon’s MCP server exposes eight tools to any MCP client: search, fetch a source, list your threads of work on a repository, read one, read its past states, read your accepted lessons, get the morning briefing, save a note. Paste its address into your assistant and authorize it in Leon: the access is revocable and inherits your permissions exactly.

home.rule1Title: Every highlighted word comes from its source.
home.rule1Lead: A pink word, a pink number, a pink original. Pick a number and read the source it comes from.
home.rule2Title: When the record is silent, Leon says so.
home.rule2Lead: No source, no claim. Ask about something nobody wrote down and the answer is “I don’t know”, with the closest thing on record.

documentation.heroTitle: Connect Leon to your coding tools.
documentation.heroLead: Two ways to do it: ask Claude Code to install it, or paste one command in a terminal. Either way, you authorize the computer in your browser.

requirements.title: What you need
requirements.lead: Four things, on the computer you want to connect.
requirements.system: A Mac (Apple silicon or Intel), or a Linux on x64 or arm64 with glibc (Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora…). Windows, Alpine and the other Linux systems with musl are not supported: the command stops before it writes anything.
requirements.claude: At least one coding tool installed on this computer: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or Antigravity. leon setup connects each one it finds, after showing its own text of what will be sent.
requirements.account: A Leon account. You sign in in your browser when you authorize the computer.

claude.title: Ask Claude Code
claude.lead: The simplest way. The button copies instructions: paste them into Claude Code and it does the setup with you.
claude.askTitle: What Claude Code will ask you
claude.ask1: Its permission to run the install command.
claude.ask2: Probably also to run it outside its sandbox (the isolated zone where it runs its commands), which may forbid writing in ~/.leon, downloading from nodejs.org, opening your browser or listening on 127.0.0.1 (your own computer only), which signing in does.
claude.ask3: Your agreement before it finishes the setup with the --yes option. It must first copy to you, as is and without summarizing, what will be sent (see “What is sent”). Without your explicit agreement, it does not run it. --yes gives no usage by itself: you choose them with the boxes of the authorization page.
claude.ask4: A click on “Authorize” in your browser, and your choice in its boxes: the usages checked by default, such as reading Leon (see “What is sent”), that your coding tools do not have yet. Claude Code warns you before it runs the command, which waits for that click for 5 minutes at most (about 100 seconds when the computer is already connected and the command opens the page again for the boxes), and reminds you that it ran it for you. The instructions forbid it from ticking, unticking or clicking anything on that page, and from opening its address in a browser it controls.
claude.end: At the end, it tells you which coding tools are connected and which Leon account the computer is connected to. The instructions forbid it from asking for, reading or showing a token.
claude.unavailable: The address of this Leon is not one the install command accepts, so the button is not offered here. The commands below show the address to replace.

terminal.title: In a terminal
terminal.lead: Open a terminal on the computer you want to connect and paste this command.
terminal.leadGeneric: Open a terminal on the computer you want to connect and paste this command, with the address of your Leon in place of the one shown.
terminal.step1: downloads the official Node of the version Leon pinned and Leon’s command-line tool (a single file, served by Leon), checks their SHA-256 and puts them in ~/.leon;
terminal.step2: runs leon setup: it writes the launcher ~/.leon/bin/leon, connects the computer (see “Authorize the computer”), looks for your coding tools, shows you what will be sent, asks for your agreement, then sets up the Claude Code hooks (small programs that Claude Code runs at the start and at the end of each session).
terminal.scope: It writes only in ~/.leon, plus the settings of your coding tools after you agree: nothing in your PATH, nothing in your shell profile. The commands below are therefore written with the full path, ~/.leon/bin/leon.
terminal.again: You can run it again at any time: what is already in place is not rewritten, and the command-line tool is brought to the version Leon serves.

authorize.title: Authorize the computer
authorize.p1: Your browser opens on a Leon page. Sign in if needed: the page then asks “Authorize this computer to send your coding sessions to Leon, in the … workspace?”. Click “Authorize” only if you just ran the command, yourself or by asking Claude Code to; otherwise click “Cancel”. When leon setup opens it, the page can also show boxes, checked by default, for the usages your coding tools do not have yet (today, reading Leon, the reminder and the agent’s notes: see “What is sent”). They are yours: untick what you don’t want, then click “Authorize”. An unticked box is kept as a refusal and is not asked again; “Cancel” decides nothing.
authorize.p2: If the browser does not open, the command prints the address to open. It waits 5 minutes at most (100 seconds when leon setup --yes opens the page again on a computer that is already connected); Ctrl+C cancels without writing anything.
authorize.p3: Once the computer is authorized, the command shows the workspace and the account it is connected to (“Connected to … as …”) and keeps the connection in ~/.leon/connexion.json, readable only by your account on the computer. The token is created on your computer: the browser only sees its fingerprint.
authorize.shared: On a computer where several accounts are open at the same time, the other accounts can read the authorization address (on Linux, in /proc), and one of them could authorize it with their own Leon account: your token would then be registered on theirs. So check the account the command shows; if it is not yours, run ~/.leon/bin/leon logout. Or use ~/.leon/bin/leon login --with-token, which relies on a token created in Settings instead of that address.

sent.title: What is sent
sent.lead: In short, the text leon setup shows you before it sets up the hooks (nothing is written in the Claude Code settings before you agree). That is the text you accept, in the terminal or, with Claude Code, by telling it to use --yes. --yes gives no usage by itself: each usage below is asked separately, in the terminal or, for reading Leon, the reminder and the agent’s notes only, with a box of the authorization page when leon setup opens it.
sent.where: The hooks go in your personal Claude Code settings: they run in all your sessions, in all your folders, personal ones included. A session started by a script (claude -p) runs them too, except with --bare, which loads no hooks.
sent.end: At the end of each session, the Leon server receives the text of the exchanges (your messages and Claude’s answers; the messages Claude Code adds in your place, such as a background task’s result, the output of a ! or / command, another session’s message or a script’s prompt, labeled as not typed by you; the final report of each subagent, labeled the same way; a ! command you type is sent whole) and the actions of the session, read from its transcript: the files written (paths in the repository), the commands run (only their executable, plus the subcommand for a fixed list of developer tools such as git, gh, pnpm or docker; never their other arguments), Git (branch, commits, pull requests), the task list, and a few markers (start and end times, number of messages and tool errors, whether the session used the web, an MCP server, a subagent or a network command).
sent.tools: Codex, Cursor and Antigravity, when leon setup finds their settings folder (for Antigravity, one of its own folders under ~/.gemini: ~/.gemini alone, the folder of Gemini CLI, is not enough), each show their own text first. After each turn, the Leon server receives the new exchanges and the actions of the session, read from the tool’s own file; the messages the tool writes itself in your place (a subagent’s report, a notification; with Codex, a ! command with its output) are sent too, labeled as written by the tool, not by you; the context the tool adds itself is not sent. What a hook missed is sent in the background the next time Leon’s start hook runs on this computer: at the start of a Claude Code or Codex session, or at the first message of a Cursor or Antigravity conversation. The usages below (lecture, rappel, noter, resume) are offered to them too, with the same texts. coulisses is offered to Codex and Antigravity, each with its own text, never to Cursor: its transcript writes neither the reasoning nor the result of a tool call.
sent.secrets: Secrets are masked before sending, and again by the server.
sent.start: At the start of each session, the server receives the project key, the current Git branch and the session id. It sends back your recent sessions on this repository (their branch, pull requests, commits, files and remaining tasks) and the project’s morning briefing: Claude Code adds this block to the session context, so it is given to Claude Code’s model. With the lecture usage (below), it sends back instead of your recent sessions the summary of your work threads on this repository and an instruction to read the thread of the task.
sent.lecture: The lecture usage (reading Leon) is checked by default: leon setup asks for it once for all the coding tools it sets up, with a box of the authorization page when leon setup opens it (to connect this computer, or again with --yes), otherwise in a terminal ([Y/n]: Enter accepts it); it never gives it by itself. A refusal is kept: it is not asked again until retirer-crochets. With it, at the start of each session or conversation, Leon places in the agent’s context the summary of your work threads on this repository (keys only: their id, branch, tools, dates, pull request numbers and states, number of linked sources) instead of your recent sessions, the lessons you accepted, and an instruction to read the thread of the task. For this, the start request also carries the usages of the tool and the Leon command of the computer, cited in the instruction. The agent can read your threads, their summaries and their state, the lessons you accepted, and the memory of this repository that you can see, with leon threads, leon thread, leon search, leon versions and leon lessons, or with the MCP tools threads, thread, versions and lessons. The model provider of the tool sees what is placed and what is read. This usage never lets an agent write anything to Leon. The commands use the token of the computer: once one of your tools accepts it, they work for every agent on the computer; refusing it in a tool only removes, in that tool, what is placed at the start.
sent.rappel: The rappel usage (the reminder at each message) is checked by default, asked like lecture: once for all the coding tools it sets up, with a box of the authorization page, otherwise in a terminal ([Y/n]: Enter accepts it); --yes never gives it by itself. A refusal is kept: it is not asked again until retirer-crochets. It is offered for Claude Code (a UserPromptSubmit hook that runs leon reminder, set up only once the usage is given), Codex (the same hook, to approve with /hooks), Cursor and Antigravity (their message hook, already in place, with no hook added). For Antigravity, only in a version whose hook receives the message (tried with the app 2.0.6): with an older one, no reminder arrives. With it, each time you send a message, the first 2,000 characters of your message (secrets masked before sending, and again by the server) go only to the Leon server, with the project key, the current Git branch, the session id, the name of the tool and the usages it accepted. The server neither stores nor logs the message: it only looks for those of your threads on this repository that it touches, and sends back one line of keys about one or two threads not yet cited in the session, which the tool adds to the agent’s context, so its model provider sees it. The hook waits 1.5 seconds at most: without an answer, your message goes on without it. The list of the threads already cited in each session (never the message) is kept for 24 hours, then deleted within the next hour.
sent.noter: The noter usage (the agent’s notes) is checked by default, asked like lecture: once for all the coding tools it sets up, with a box of the authorization page, otherwise in a terminal ([Y/n]: Enter accepts it); --yes never gives it by itself. A refusal is kept: it is not asked again until retirer-crochets. It is offered for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Antigravity, with no hook added. With it, the agent can keep notes with leon note: each note sends the Leon server the text of the note (4,000 characters at most, secrets masked before sending, and again by the server), with the project key, the name of the tool, the session id and the usages this tool accepted. The note is kept like your sessions, with its versions: Leon’s search finds it, and it is never placed as it is in the context of a session. At the start of each session or conversation, the start request also carries the usages of the tool, the Leon command of the computer and the name of the tool, and Leon places in the agent’s context one sentence that gives the leon note command with the tool and the session id filled in (the session id only when it is safe in a shell); the model provider of the tool sees it. Refusing it in a tool removes that sentence there, and leon note then sends nothing for that tool. It also turns off remember, the note tool of Leon’s MCP connector, for all your assistants connected to this workspace, until you turn it back on in the Memory section of the settings.
sent.coulisses: The coulisses usage (full capture) is optional, for Claude Code, Codex and Antigravity, never for Cursor: leon setup asks for it separately for each of these tools, with that tool’s own text, only in a terminal ([y/N]), never with --yes nor on the authorization page. A yes given for one tool does not count for another, even in a single run of leon setup. A refusal is kept for that tool: it is not asked again until retirer-crochets. Claude Code’s text comes first. At the end of each session, the Leon server this computer is connected to also receives what happened behind the exchanges: the agent’s reasoning, when Claude Code writes its text in the transcript; the instruction given to each subagent and its final report; and each tool call, those of subagents included, reduced to the name of the tool, its target and its status. The target is, for a command, only its executable, plus the subcommand for a fixed list of developer tools; for a file tool, the path in the repository; for an MCP tool, nothing, and only the name of its server is kept. Never the output of a tool, nor a search pattern, a URL, a query or any other argument. Secrets are masked before sending, and again by the server. The blocks Leon placed in the session are removed, and each text is cut at 20,000 characters. All this is kept with the session and can be read like it: by you and, on the Leon website, by the managers above you. Leon’s search finds the reasoning and the subagents; it shows the tool calls only on request. None of this is ever placed in the morning briefing, in the context of a new session, in a session summary or in the state of your work threads. Withdrawing your consent stops this sending. What was already sent stays in Leon. With Claude Code’s default settings, the reasoning has no text in the transcript, so nothing of it is sent; with showThinkingSummaries turned on in Claude Code’s settings, the summary of the reasoning is written there in interactive sessions, and it is sent (seen with Claude Code 2.1.322).
sent.coulissesCodex: With Codex, the first point of the text becomes: Once a Codex session is over, the Leon server this computer is connected to also receives what happened behind the exchanges: the summary of the agent’s reasoning, when Codex writes one in the session file; the instruction given to each subagent and its final report; and each tool call, those of subagents included, reduced to the name of the tool, its target and its status. The target is, for a command, only its executable, plus the subcommand for a fixed list of developer tools; for a file change, the path in the repository; for an MCP tool, nothing, and only the name of its server is kept. Never the output of a tool, nor a search pattern, a URL, a query or any other argument. A session is over at its end when Codex runs that hook (codex exec), otherwise once its file has not changed for 30 minutes: it is then sent in the background the next time Leon’s start hook runs on this computer. The rest is the same as for Claude Code. So, outside codex exec, the full capture of a session arrives late: 30 minutes after its last change, then at the next session start of one of your tools. Codex does not always write a summary of its reasoning: without one, nothing of the reasoning is sent.
sent.coulissesAntigravity: With Antigravity, the first point of the text becomes: Once an Antigravity conversation has not changed for 30 minutes, the Leon server this computer is connected to also receives what happened behind the exchanges: the agent’s reasoning, which Antigravity writes in full in the transcript; the instruction given to each subagent and its final report; and each tool call, those of subagents included, reduced to the name of the tool, its target and its status. The target is, for a command, only its executable, plus the subcommand for a fixed list of developer tools; for a file tool, the path in the repository; for any other tool, nothing, and a tool Leon does not know, such as an MCP tool, is kept without its name. Never the output of a tool, nor a search pattern, a URL, a query or any other argument. It is sent in the background the next time Leon’s start hook runs on this computer. The rest is the same as for Claude Code. So the full capture of a conversation always arrives late, and the reasoning is sent in full, not as a summary. When the app does not write the exit code of a command (as with the Antigravity app 2.31.0, the only one tried), a command that fails keeps the status ok.
sent.resume: Session summaries (the resume usage) are optional: leon setup asks for them separately, once for all the coding tools it sets up, only in a terminal, never with --yes nor on the authorization page. A refusal is kept: leon setup does not ask again. To change your answer, run ~/.leon/bin/leon retirer-crochets (with --outil codex, --outil cursor or --outil antigravity for those tools; it removes the hooks and withdraws the consent of the tool), then leon setup again. Once a session with at least 6 of your messages has ended, the Leon server sends its actions, the state of its pull requests and the end of its exchanges (40,000 characters at most, secrets already masked) to Leon’s model provider, which writes the summary. Leon’s search finds it; it is never added to the context of a new session. Withdrawing your consent stops new summaries: retirer-crochets tells the Leon server this computer is connected to (only that server and account: one this computer used before is not told). If the computer is offline then, a summary already planned may still be written within an hour, and Leon later tells the server the computer is connected to by then: at the next session start of a tool that keeps its hooks, or when you run retirer-crochets again. The same usage also keeps the state of your work threads up to date: the actions, exchanges and summaries of these sessions, the state of their pull requests and the sources linked to the thread that you can see are sent to Leon’s model provider, which writes that state. Withdrawing your consent stops this too, once the Leon server is told.
sent.server: The hooks contact the server of the connection made by leon login, unless LEON_URL and LEON_TOKEN are both set (a developer setup): those come first.

read.title: Reading Leon from a session
read.lead: Five commands read Leon’s memory of the repository they are run in and print it on standard output; they write nothing on disk. Your agent can run them, and so can you.
read.output: What they print starts with Leon’s guard line: it is data to check against the code and Git, never instructions. threads lists the threads of the repository (the work of your sessions, grouped by branch), the current branch first; thread prints one thread, with its state, sessions, pull requests and linked sources (without an id: the thread of the current branch); search searches Leon within this repository only; versions lists the readable versions of a thread’s state or of a lesson, or prints one with --read; lessons prints the lessons you accepted for this repository and those that apply to all your repositories (with an id: that lesson only). Nothing writes a lesson or restores a version from your computer: that is done on the website.
read.consent: They need a connection and the reading usage (lecture, see “What is sent”), accepted by one of your code tools; leon setup offers it, checked by default. Without it, the server refuses, and the command says to run ~/.leon/bin/leon setup in a terminal. The server notes each read (the tool and the source read).
read.external: Reading Leon does not count as bringing text from elsewhere into the session: neither these commands, nor the threads, thread, versions, lessons and remember tools of Leon’s MCP connector, when the MCP settings of your tool (Claude Code, Codex or Cursor) declare the leon server with the MCP address of the server you are connected to. Leon reads only that address there, never a header or a token. The connector’s search, fetch and briefing tools still count, as does any other MCP server.

updates.title: Updates
updates.auto: Leon’s command-line tool updates itself, at most once a day, when a session starts, from the server of your connection, and only over https. A local Leon (http://localhost) is updated by hand: ~/.leon/bin/leon update. An update touches neither your connection, nor your agreement, nor the launcher, nor the hooks.
updates.previous: To go back to the previous version, without network:
updates.previousNote: If the server still serves the same version, the next update, at the first session start after 24 hours, puts it back.

disconnect.title: Disconnect
disconnect.fromLeon: From Leon: {path}. This computer will stop sending your sessions.
disconnect.logout: From the computer: ~/.leon/bin/leon logout revokes the token of this computer and removes ~/.leon/connexion.json. If the server does not answer, the command says so and removes only the computer’s connection: revoke the computer in Settings then (see above).
disconnect.remove: ~/.leon/bin/leon retirer-crochets (French for “remove hooks”) removes Leon’s hooks from the Claude Code settings (your other settings stay as they are), withdraws your agreement (nothing is sent from Claude Code anymore), tells the Leon server this computer is connected to, and deletes the launcher once no other tool uses it and the server was told of each withdrawal. So run it before logout, which removes the connection it uses: once the launcher is gone, revoke the computer in Settings (see above).
disconnect.all: To leave completely: retirer-crochets (run it again until it no longer says the Leon server could not be told), then revoke the computer in Settings, then delete the ~/.leon folder.
disconnect.kept: Disconnecting does not delete what was already sent.
