findMessage.title: Leon seems to do nothing: find its message first
findMessage.text: You see: nothing from Leon. No block at the start of a session, no reminder, no error. Why: Leon’s hooks never get in your tool’s way, with one deliberate exception: with the usage passage, the first change of a file in a Claude Code session is stopped once (this is the entry “Leon : cette modification attend.” below). They always exit with code 0, and they write their errors only on standard error, which Claude Code does not show. A command you run by hand exits with code 1 on a usage error (a wrong option or argument), and most also do on a failure they report; the read and note commands exit with 0 even when the server fails. To check: open a terminal outside Cursor (in Cursor’s terminal, Leon’s Claude Code commands stay silent on purpose), go to the folder of the project and run ~/.leon/bin/leon briefing. If a block appears, the connection and the server work, at least from this terminal: a terminal sees LEON_URL and LEON_TOKEN, a tool started from the Dock does not (see “It works in a terminal, not in your tool”). Otherwise, a line, most often starting with “Leon:”, gives the cause. Run ~/.leon/bin/leon threads the same way to test reading. What to do: look for that line in the entries below. These lines are fixed texts: they never contain your token or the text of a session, so you can paste them to an agent. There is no leon status or leon doctor command. Words used below: the start block is what Leon adds to the context at the start of a session (at the first message, in Cursor and Antigravity); the catch-up is the background task that sends what a hook of Codex, Cursor or Antigravity missed; ~/.claude stands for the settings folder of Claude Code, $CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR if you set it.

browser.title: The browser is on another computer
browser.text: You see: leon login waits, then ends with “Timed out: the browser did not come back within 5 minutes. Nothing was saved.” Why: the browser is on another computer, for example over SSH or in a remote container, so the return to 127.0.0.1 never arrives. What to do: create a token in {path}, then, on the computer you want to connect:
browser.after: Paste the token when the command asks for it (it is not shown as you type), then finish with ~/.leon/bin/leon setup.

noTerminal.title: “No terminal is available”
noTerminal.text: You see: the install command ends with “No terminal is available to ask you questions. To finish, open a terminal and run:”, followed by a command. Why: the script put Node and the command-line tool in place, but it has no terminal to ask you its questions (this is the case from Claude Code or from a script). What to do: run the command it prints in a terminal.

platform.title: The install script refuses this computer
platform.text: You see: the script answers “not supported yet” (Windows, another architecture), or says your Linux uses musl (Alpine). Why: Leon supports macOS, and Linux with glibc, on x64 and arm64. The script stops before writing anything. What to do: use a Mac, or a Linux with glibc.

installFailed.title: The install command stops with “leon install:”
installFailed.text: You see: a line that starts with “leon install:”, such as “'curl' is required but was not found on this computer.”, “could not download … Check your network, and that … is allowed through any proxy or firewall.”, “… does not match its SHA-256. Nothing was installed.”, “could not unpack Node (is 'xz' installed?). Nothing was installed.” or “the Node that was downloaded does not start on this computer.” Why: a tool is missing, the network or a proxy blocks a download, or the file that arrived is not the expected one. The script checks everything before it puts anything in place. To check: which curl tar xz. What to do: install what is missing (xz is needed on Linux), let through the host that the message names, then run the install command again. If it says “the setup did not finish. To resume it, run: …”, run the command it prints.

revoked.title: Computer revoked, or token refused
revoked.text: You see: “Leon: token refused by the Leon server.” (reading, notes), “Leon: token refused by the server, session not captured.” (end of a session), “Leon: briefing unavailable (server unreachable or token refused).” (start of a session) or “Token refused by the Leon server.” (import). Why: the server no longer accepts the token of this computer. The computer was revoked in Settings, or the token belongs to another Leon server. To check: ~/.leon/bin/leon setup then says “This computer was disconnected from Leon (its token was revoked): connecting it again.” What to do: run the install command again, or ~/.leon/bin/leon setup: it sees the computer is no longer connected and starts the connection again. If the refusal comes back after that, see “Old LEON_URL and LEON_TOKEN still apply”.

interrupted.title: Still not connected after creating a workspace or resetting your password
interrupted.text: You see: you had to create a workspace or reset your password while authorizing, and the computer is still not connected. Why: those paths lose the authorization in progress. What to do: start the connection again with ~/.leon/bin/leon login, then finish with ~/.leon/bin/leon setup.

notConnected.title: “This computer is not connected”
notConnected.text: You see: “Leon: LEON_URL is missing or invalid (https, or http on localhost and 127.0.0.1). LEON_TOKEN is missing or invalid (a token created in Leon, shaped like leon_…). This computer is not connected: run ~/.leon/bin/leon login (pnpm leon login from a clone).” Sometimes only one of the first two sentences shows. If a sentence about LEON_URL or LEON_TOKEN shows without “This computer is not connected”, both variables are set and one of them is invalid: the saved connection is then ignored, and leon login changes nothing (see “Old LEON_URL and LEON_TOKEN still apply”). The read and note commands print it; the hooks then do nothing. Why: no connection is saved, and LEON_URL and LEON_TOKEN are not both set. A saved connection that is unreadable, invalid or a symbolic link counts as missing. To check: ls -l ~/.leon/connexion.json must show a regular file that only you can read (-rw-------). Do not open it: it holds your token. What to do: run ~/.leon/bin/leon login, then ~/.leon/bin/leon setup. If the browser is on another computer, see “The browser is on another computer”.

envFirst.title: Old LEON_URL and LEON_TOKEN still apply
envFirst.text: You see: after a successful leon login, the commands still say “Leon: token refused by the Leon server.”, or your sessions go to another server. Or every command prints only “Leon: LEON_TOKEN is missing or invalid (…)” (or the same about LEON_URL), without “This computer is not connected”. leon login printed “Note: LEON_URL and LEON_TOKEN are both set in your environment. They keep being used before the connection that leon login saves.” Why: when both variables are set, they come before the saved connection. So an old token in your shell profile or in an editor’s settings keeps being used, and a malformed value (a token cut short, an http address) stops every command, even with a valid saved connection. LEON_URL alone also picks the server of leon login when you give no --url. From a Leon clone, pnpm leon also reads them from the clone’s .env.local. leon setup checks only the saved connection: it can say all is well while the hooks send with a refused token. To check: printenv LEON_URL shows the address only (never print LEON_TOKEN). In a clone, grep -c '^LEON_TOKEN=' .env.local counts the line without showing it. What to do: run unset LEON_URL LEON_TOKEN, then remove them from your shell profile, your editor or the .env.local. These variables are only for tests and clones. Then send the missed sessions again with ~/.leon/bin/leon import-claude-code --project followed by the folder, and --since followed by a date (see “A Claude Code session did not arrive”): the server ignores what it already has.

wrongAccount.title: Sessions go to another account or workspace
wrongAccount.text: You see: your sessions do not show up in your Leon. Or leon setup says “The authorization page was approved from another account or workspace than the one this computer is connected to: nothing was changed, and the new authorization was revoked.” Why: the authorization page links the computer to the account and the workspace open in the browser at that moment. If that is the wrong account, the token of the computer is registered there. When leon setup opens the page again on a connected computer, it requires the same account and the same workspace. To check: the last line of leon login, “Connected to … as … (this computer: …)”. On the website, with your account, the computer must be listed in Settings › Integrations › Connected computers. What to do: open the website with the right account and workspace, run ~/.leon/bin/leon logout, then ~/.leon/bin/leon login. On a shared computer, prefer ~/.leon/bin/leon login --with-token. Sessions already sent to the wrong account stay there.

loginFailed.title: leon login does not finish
loginFailed.text: You see one of: “Timed out: the browser did not come back within 5 minutes. Nothing was saved.”, “Authorization cancelled in the browser. Nothing was saved.”, “Could not listen on 127.0.0.1 (…). Run leon login --with-token instead.”, “The server refused the authorization (it is valid once, for 2 minutes).”, “This authorization was already used.”, “The server could not register this computer (HTTP …).” Then leon setup says “Leon: setup stopped: this computer is not connected, so no hook was installed.” Why: the browser did not send the code back to 127.0.0.1 in time, the page was cancelled, or the code was used late or twice. Each code is valid once, for 2 minutes. To check: the browser that opened must be on this computer. What to do: run ~/.leon/bin/leon login again: each try gets a new code. Without a browser on this computer, see “The browser is on another computer”. Then run ~/.leon/bin/leon setup.

loginRefused.title: leon login refuses the address or the token
loginRefused.text: You see: “No server address: pass --url …, or set LEON_URL.”, “…: not a valid address (https, or http on localhost and 127.0.0.1).”, “That is not a Leon token (it is shaped like leon_…). Create one in Settings.”, “The server refused this token: it may be revoked, or belong to another Leon.”, “Could not reach the server. Check the address and your network, then try again.” or “leon login takes no argument: --with-token reads the token from the standard input, never from the command line. …” Why: the address is missing or is not https (http works only on localhost and 127.0.0.1). Or the pasted token is malformed, revoked or from another server. Or a token was typed on the command line. To check: the address of your Leon starts with https. What to do: run ~/.leon/bin/leon login --url followed by the address of your Leon. With a token, run ~/.leon/bin/leon login --with-token, then paste it when asked. A token typed on the command line is now in your shell history: revoke it in Settings › Integrations › Personal tokens and create another.

setupStops.title: leon setup stops before writing anything
setupStops.text: You see: “Leon: Leon is not installed in ~/.leon (there is no Node or no CLI there), so its launcher would not run. …”, “Leon: --depot: this folder is not a Leon repository.”, “Leon: CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR must be an absolute path.”, or “… already exists and is different. … Replace it? [y/N]”. Why: the Node and the command line that the install script puts in ~/.leon are missing (an unfinished install, or a deleted folder). Or --depot does not point to a Leon clone. Or CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR is a relative path. Or the launcher ~/.leon/bin/leon holds something else than what Leon would write: Leon shows both and asks. To check: ls -l ~/.leon/runtime/actuel/node ~/.leon/cli/actuelle/leon.mjs. What to do: run the install command again. Give CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR an absolute path, and --depot a Leon clone. For the launcher, answer y after reading the comparison, or move the file away and run the install command again.

settingsFile.title: Leon cannot read or write the settings of your tool
settingsFile.text: You see: “Leon: … is unreadable or does not have the expected shape. …”, “… is unreadable: it is not a valid JSON object (Claude Code reads strict JSON, with no comments or trailing commas) or the file is inaccessible …”, or “Leon: could not write …”. Why: the settings file of the tool (settings.json for Claude Code, hooks.json for Codex, Cursor and Antigravity) has a comment or a trailing comma, a section of another shape, wrong permissions, or the disk is full. Leon writes nothing rather than risk your settings. When only ~/.leon/accord.json could not be written, the hooks are in place but send nothing, or only the text of the exchanges. To check: the file named in the message must be strict JSON. What to do: fix the file, the permissions or the disk space, then run ~/.leon/bin/leon setup again: it is safe to run again. Do not edit ~/.leon/accord.json by hand: an unreadable one counts as a withdrawal.

pageNotAnswered.title: leon setup --yes added no usage
pageNotAnswered.text: You see: “Nothing was chosen on the authorization page: this computer stays connected as before, and no usage was added. …” or “This computer was connected with leon login --with-token: leon setup --yes does not open the authorization page. …” Why: on a connected computer, leon setup --yes opens the authorization page again for the usages not chosen yet. The page was cancelled, refused, left for more than 100 seconds, or approved from another account. A computer connected with a token cannot open that page. What to do: run ~/.leon/bin/leon setup in a terminal, without --yes: it asks its questions there.

updateFailed.title: Leon does not update
updateFailed.text: You see: “Leon: this Leon runs from a clone: update it with git. Nothing was changed.”, “Leon: could not read the latest version of Leon from the server.”, “Leon: could not unpack Node (is xz installed?).”, a size or SHA-256 mismatch, or “… does not start.” Or no message at all: Leon just stays at its version. Why: a clone is updated with git, never by Leon. The automatic update runs in the background, at most once a day, and says nothing. It needs a connection saved by leon login, over https: an http connection, or LEON_URL and LEON_TOKEN alone, get none. A download that fails its checks leaves the current version in place. To check: run ~/.leon/bin/leon update by hand: it prints each failure. What to do: fix what it names (on Linux, install xz), then run it again. ~/.leon/bin/leon update --previous goes back to the version before, until the automatic update brings the served version back, 24 hours later at the earliest. If nothing starts anymore, run the install command again.

serverNotTold.title: “The Leon server could not be told”
serverNotTold.text: You see: “Leon: the Leon server could not be told of this withdrawal …”, “Leon: the Leon server refused the token of this computer, so it could not be told of this withdrawal. …”, “Leon: the Leon server could not be told of this refusal … remember stays on for the assistants connected to this workspace. …”, or, at leon logout, “Could not reach the server, or it did not answer as expected: the token of this computer was not revoked there. Revoke it in Settings.” Why: the change is written on the computer first. The server learns it only if it answers and accepts the token of the computer. A withdrawal is told later: at the next session start of a tool that keeps its hooks, or when you run the command again. What to do: if the token is refused, run ~/.leon/bin/leon login first. To tell a withdrawal now, run the same command again, with the same --outil as the first time, or without it if it was Claude Code: without --outil, leon retirer-crochets withdraws Claude Code. A refusal of remember is not told again: turn remember off in Settings › Memory, on the website. After such a logout, revoke the computer in Settings › Integrations › Connected computers.

envOnly.title: It works in a terminal, not in your tool
envOnly.text: You see: leon setup says “This computer is connected only by LEON_URL and LEON_TOKEN, which a Claude Code started from the Dock or an editor does not see: running ~/.leon/bin/leon login.” Or the commands work in your terminal while the hooks do nothing. Why: an environment variable exists only in the shell where it was set. A Claude Code started from the Dock or from an editor does not see it, so its hooks have no connection. Only the connection saved by leon login is seen by every tool. To check: ls -l ~/.leon/connexion.json shows whether a connection is saved. What to do: let leon setup run leon login (it does it by itself), or run ~/.leon/bin/leon login yourself.

disableAllHooks.title: Claude Code runs no hooks
disableAllHooks.text: You see: leon setup warns “Warning: "disableAllHooks" is true in these settings; as long as it stays that way, Claude Code runs no hooks.” Or Leon’s hooks are installed but never run. Why: that setting turns off every hook, Leon’s included. Settings managed by your company can do the same: disableAllHooks there, or allowManagedHooksOnly, which runs only the hooks the company sets. And a Claude Code that reads another settings folder than the one leon setup wrote to (CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR set for one and not for the other) never sees Leon’s hooks. To check: /hooks in Claude Code lists the active hooks and the file of each. Look for disableAllHooks in your Claude Code settings (user, project and local project). What to do: remove that setting or set it to false, then restart Claude Code. Managed settings change only through whoever manages them. Run leon setup with the same CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR as Claude Code.

trustFolder.title: Leon does nothing in a folder you just opened
trustFolder.text: You see: in a folder you open for the first time in Claude Code, Leon does nothing: no block, no reminder, nothing captured at the end. Why: in an interactive session, Claude Code runs the hooks of a folder only once you trust that folder, in the window it shows at the first opening. A claude -p session never shows that window and counts the folder as trusted. This is Claude Code’s own rule, from its hooks documentation (“Workspace trust”). To check: open Claude Code in that folder again: the window must not show anymore. What to do: trust the folder. A session that ran without hooks can be sent later with ~/.leon/bin/leon import-claude-code --project followed by the folder (see “A Claude Code session did not arrive”).

cloneForm.title: From a Leon clone, the hooks fail
cloneForm.text: You see: at install, “Warning: … is a temporary Git worktree: if it is deleted, the hooks will stop working. …” or “Warning: …/.env.local does not give the commands what they need to reach the server: …”. Or the hooks fail or run out of time when Claude Code is started from an editor or an app. Why: in the clone form, the launcher runs pnpm in your clone. It needs the pnpm version pinned in package.json, and node 24 or later, on the PATH that Claude Code sees. A deleted worktree breaks the command of the hooks. To check: which pnpm node and node --version, in the environment that starts Claude Code. What to do: use the installed form, which brings its own Node: ~/.leon/bin/leon setup, without --depot. Or set up the clone form from the main clone, never from a worktree.

consentWithdrawn.title: “Your consent for Claude Code was withdrawn”
consentWithdrawn.text: You see: “Leon: your consent for Claude Code was withdrawn (leon retirer-crochets): nothing is sent. To give it again, run ~/.leon/bin/leon setup …”. Or leon setup says “The Leon hooks are already in place in …, but your consent was withdrawn: for now, they send nothing.” Why: your consent on this computer was withdrawn by leon retirer-crochets, or ~/.leon/accord.json is unreadable: an unreadable file counts as a withdrawal. Then nothing is captured, and no block or reminder arrives. When leon setup says “… but your consent is not recorded …”, only the text of the exchanges is sent. To check: ls -l ~/.leon/accord.json. What to do: run ~/.leon/bin/leon setup in a terminal: it asks for your consent again, without touching your settings. If ~/.leon/bin/leon is gone, run the install command again. Do not edit ~/.leon/accord.json by hand.

noConsentTool.title: “No consent recorded” for Codex, Cursor or Antigravity
noConsentTool.text: You see: “Leon: no consent recorded for Codex: nothing is sent.” at the start, or “Leon: no consent recorded for the capture of Codex: nothing is sent.” (the same with Cursor or Antigravity). Why: this tool has no consent on this computer. It was never given, or it was withdrawn with leon retirer-crochets --outil. Unlike Claude Code, these tools send nothing at all without it. To check: the name of the tool shows in the message. What to do: run ~/.leon/bin/leon setup in a terminal and answer yes for that tool.

noReminder.title: No reminder under your message
noReminder.text: You see: no reminder of your threads reaches the agent after your message, and no error. Why: the reminder is quiet by design. It needs the rappel usage for that tool. It cites a thread only when your message names its branch or one of its files in full (a name with a /, _, . or -), or shares at least two useful words with it. It looks only at your 100 most recent threads on the repository, cites two at most, and cites a thread only once per session. It gives up after 1.5 seconds without an answer. Cursor and Antigravity send it only when a folder is open, and Antigravity only from its app 2.0.6 on. To check: run ~/.leon/bin/leon setup in a terminal: it offers the usages a tool is missing. What to do: name the branch, a file or a few words of the thread in your message. Or read it directly: ~/.leon/bin/leon threads, then ~/.leon/bin/leon thread followed by its id.

unreachable.title: “Server unreachable or too slow”
unreachable.text: You see: “Leon: leon thread unavailable (server unreachable or too slow).” (or threads, search, versions, lessons, note), “Leon: briefing unavailable (server unreachable or token refused).”, or at the end of a session “Leon: server too slow (timeout exceeded), session not captured.” or “Leon: server unreachable or unexpected response, session not captured.” For the reminder there is no message: the line is just missing. A message with “response … from the server” gives the HTTP code the server sent. Why: the server did not answer in time, or at all: no network, a VPN, a server that is down, or a wrong address. Behind a proxy that is the only way out, the install goes through (curl uses HTTPS_PROXY) but Leon’s commands do not: Leon’s Node ignores HTTPS_PROXY unless NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1 is also set. Leon waits 3 seconds for the start block, 1.5 seconds for the reminder, 10 seconds for a note, 15 seconds to send a session and 30 seconds for a read. Inside the Claude Code sandbox, the same message comes for another reason: see “Reads fail inside the Claude Code sandbox”. To check: run ~/.leon/bin/leon threads in a terminal, outside any sandbox. If it fails the same way, this computer cannot reach the server. What to do: fix the network or the address. Behind such a proxy, set NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1 wherever HTTPS_PROXY is set. A session that was not sent stays on the computer: for Claude Code, send it with ~/.leon/bin/leon import-claude-code --project followed by the folder (see “A Claude Code session did not arrive”); for the other tools, the next catch-up sends it. The start block and the reminder are not replayed.

serverOlder.title: The server is older than the command line
serverOlder.text: You see: “Leon: this Leon server does not have leon thread yet (route missing).” (or another read command, or leon note), “Leon: this server does not prepare a morning briefing yet (route missing).”, “Leon: the server does not recognize this upload (it may be older than the CLI), session not captured.”, “the server does not accept session facts (it may be older than the CLI), only the turns were sent.”, “the server does not accept the full capture of sessions (it may be older than the CLI), the turns were sent.”, or “unavailable (response 400 from the server)”. Why: the command line on this computer is newer than the server. The server checks each request strictly, so it refuses a field or a usage it does not know. This happens with a clone ahead of the server, with a server that was rolled back, or with a connection to another, older server. To check: the message names the command or the sending the server refused. What to do: the server must be deployed before the command line. On an installed computer, ~/.leon/bin/leon update brings the version that the server serves. A clone is updated with git. The turns already sent stay received; the rest leaves again at the next import or catch-up.

sessionMissing.title: A Claude Code session did not arrive
sessionMissing.text: You see: a recent Claude Code session is missing from Leon. On the standard error of the end hook: “Leon: could not read the hook input, session not captured.”, “Leon: session file not found or unreadable, session not captured.”, “Leon: nothing to send for this session.” or “Leon: capture failed (unexpected error).” Why: a session is sent by the end-of-session hook. It did not run or did not finish: a window closed by force, a crash, a computer turned off, no network, a refused token. A session opened then closed without a message has nothing to send. Sessions from before the install were never sent. By default, Claude Code deletes a transcript after 30 days without activity (cleanupPeriodDays): such a session can no longer be sent. The background catch-up does not cover Claude Code. To check: the import below ends with a line such as “… sessions, … turns sent: … new, … already known, … failures.” What to do: run ~/.leon/bin/leon import-claude-code --project followed by the folder of the project, and --since followed by the day of the first missing session (such as 2026-11-01). Without these options, the import sends the text of every session still on this computer, in all your folders, those from before the install included; their actions leave only for files changed after your consent. It is safe to run again: turns already received are not sent twice.

partialCapture.title: The exchanges arrived, not the actions or the backstage
partialCapture.text: You see: a session has its exchanges in Leon, but not its actions (files, commands, pull requests) or its backstage. Messages: “Leon: session facts not sent (server unreachable, too slow or unexpected response).”, “Leon: full capture of the session not sent (server unreachable, too slow or unexpected response).”, “the server does not accept session facts (it may be older than the CLI), only the turns were sent.” or “the server does not accept the full capture of sessions (it may be older than the CLI), the turns were sent.” Why: the exchanges, the actions and the backstage each leave in their own sending, so one can fail without the others. The 15 seconds given to send a session can also run out. The backstage needs the coulisses usage. To check: the import of Claude Code says each failure. What to do: for Claude Code, run the import again (see “A Claude Code session did not arrive”): it sends the backstage of a session only once that session has been idle for 30 minutes. For Codex, Cursor and Antigravity, the next catch-up sends what is missing. Check the usages with ~/.leon/bin/leon setup.

importOld.title: Imported sessions lack their actions, or the import reports failures
importOld.text: You see: sessions imported with leon import-claude-code have only their exchanges, without files or pull requests. Or the import ends with “… failures.” and exits with code 1. Or it says “--since expects a date in the format YYYY-MM-DD.” Why: the actions are sent only for session files changed after the date of your consent, and each usage only after its own date. An older session sends only its exchanges. To check: the last line of the import counts the sessions, the new turns, those already known and the failures. What to do: nothing can be replayed for the actions of older sessions. For failures, run the import again: it is safe to repeat. --since takes a date such as 2026-11-01.

catchUp.title: Codex, Cursor or Antigravity sessions arrive late
catchUp.text: You see: a Codex, Cursor or Antigravity session is not in Leon yet, with no message anywhere. Why: what a hook missed is sent by a catch-up that runs in the background. It starts only with Leon’s start hook: at the start of a Claude Code or Codex session, or at the first message of a Cursor or Antigravity conversation. Its output is thrown away, and only one runs at a time. It covers only the tools whose capture you accepted. To check: run ~/.leon/bin/leon rattraper by hand. It prints “Leon: … sessions caught up, … failures.” and exits with code 1 when something failed. What to do: open a new session in one of your tools, or run that command. If a tool is missing, run ~/.leon/bin/leon setup and accept its capture.

agentDoesNotRead.title: The agent never reads the memory by itself
agentDoesNotRead.text: You see: the agent never runs leon thread or leon search, even when the start block lists your threads and asks it to read the one of its task. Why: this was measured. Over 30 runs, no agent read the memory, even after the instruction was rewritten to say what the memory is for. An agent does not read what it is only shown. To check: the session has no leon thread or leon search command. What to do: ask for it in your message, for example “read the Leon thread first”. In Claude Code, the passage usage makes the agent read before its first file change. Run ~/.leon/bin/leon setup in a terminal and answer y to “Before the first change of a file in each Claude Code session you lead, have the agent read Leon first …? [y/N]”. It is asked only in a terminal, never with --yes nor on the authorization page, and it needs the lecture usage. So an agent that installs Leon for you never sets it. Codex, Cursor and Antigravity have no such option.

readFirstStop.title: “Leon : cette modification attend.”
readFirstStop.text: You see: at the first file change of a Claude Code session, the app shows that a hook blocked it, and the change is not applied. The model gets an error that contains “Leon : cette modification attend.” (the message is in French: “Leon: this change is waiting.”). Why: this is not a failure. It is the passage usage: Leon stops the first change once per session and asks the agent to read the memory first. An empty file per session in ~/.leon/temoins/claude_code makes sure it stops only once. When several changes come in one message, only one is refused. In a repository with no memory, the stop costs one turn for nothing. To check: grep -n read-first ~/.claude/settings.json shows Leon’s PreToolUse hook. What to do: nothing: the agent reads, makes its change again, and the next ones go through. To turn it off on this computer: ~/.leon/bin/leon retirer-crochets --usage passage. The other hooks and usages stay.

readFirstNoStop.title: The read-first stop never comes
readFirstNoStop.text: You see: the passage usage is accepted, but no change is ever stopped. Why: Leon stops only sessions that you lead, in the desktop app or the terminal. It does not stop subagents, nor the agents of a workflow. It does not stop claude -p or Agent SDK scripts, except a claude -p started from a session of the desktop app. It lets through a file outside the folder where the session started, or inside ~/.claude, such as a worktree stored elsewhere. It lets through writes made through Bash (sed -i, a redirection, git apply). It stops a session only once. It also lets the change through when lecture is missing, or when its marker file cannot be written. And it never runs when its hook was not written, for example because the settings file was unreadable when you accepted the usage. So a session where only subagents change files is never stopped. To check: grep -n passage ~/.leon/accord.json shows the usage under claude_code. grep -n read-first ~/.claude/settings.json, or /hooks in Claude Code, shows the hook. After a stop, a file appears in ~/.leon/temoins/claude_code. What to do: if the hook is missing, run ~/.leon/bin/leon setup again; otherwise, nothing needs repair. To try it, open a session you lead, never from inside another session’s sandbox. To be stopped again in a session, delete its file in ~/.leon/temoins/claude_code: its name is the first 32 characters of the SHA-256 of the session id (the name of the session’s transcript, without .jsonl). Files older than 7 days are deleted anyway.

readFirstLoop.title: Every file change is blocked
readFirstLoop.text: You see: in Claude Code, writes are blocked again and again by a PreToolUse hook. The model sees the hook’s command and its error, and ends up giving up the task. Or standard error says “Leon: read-first skipped (hook input missing or unreadable).” or “Leon: read-first unavailable (unexpected error).” Why: Claude Code takes a hook that exits with code 2 as a refusal, not as an error. A broken hook command (for example one where the shell cannot read an apostrophe) exits with 2 and blocks every write. leon read-first itself always exits with 0, and lets the change through when it fails. To check: /hooks shows the active command. grep -n read-first ~/.claude/settings.json must show the Leon command followed by read-first, with no argument. What to do: run ~/.leon/bin/leon retirer-crochets --usage passage, then ~/.leon/bin/leon setup to set the hook again. Never edit the hook’s command by hand.

unrelatedReminder.title: The reminder cites unrelated threads
unrelatedReminder.text: You see: on a message you did not type (a task notification, an automatic event), the agent gets a line in a rappel-leon tag, starting with “Leon : ce message touche peut-être” (“Leon: this message may touch”), that cites threads that have nothing to do with it. Why: the reminder hook sends every message the tool submits, including those the tool adds itself. The server cites a thread as soon as two useful words, or a branch or file name, match. These thresholds are still provisional, and nothing filters those messages yet. To check: the cited threads share a word or a file name with the message. What to do: nothing breaks: the line carries only thread keys, given as data, and the agent can ignore it. The reminder cannot be turned off alone yet. The only way today: ~/.leon/bin/leon retirer-crochets (with --outil and the tool, for Codex, Cursor or Antigravity) removes all the hooks of the tool, then ~/.leon/bin/leon setup lets you refuse rappel. Beware: that withdrawal also tells the server to clear the usages of the sessions this tool already sent: they get no new summary, their thread states fall back to lists, and a new consent does not give those usages back.

readingNotAllowed.title: “None of your code tools has accepted reading Leon”
readingNotAllowed.text: You see: “Leon: none of your code tools has accepted reading Leon from this computer (the lecture consent): nothing was read. …” Why: the server answers 403, because no coding tool of this computer has the lecture usage. It was never accepted, or it was refused, and a refused usage is not asked again until its tool is removed. To check: in ~/.leon/accord.json, lecture must appear under usages, not under refus. What to do: run ~/.leon/bin/leon setup in a terminal and accept it. After a refusal, first run ~/.leon/bin/leon retirer-crochets (with --outil and the tool, for Codex, Cursor or Antigravity), then ~/.leon/bin/leon setup. Beware: that withdrawal also tells the server to clear the usages of the sessions this tool already sent: they get no new summary, their thread states fall back to lists, and a new consent does not give those usages back.

sandbox.title: Reads fail inside the Claude Code sandbox
sandbox.text: You see: in a Claude Code session with its sandbox on (sandbox.enabled), the agent’s leon thread or leon search prints “Leon: leon thread unavailable (server unreachable or too slow).”, while the same command works in your terminal. After a read-first stop, the agent makes its change without having read. Why: the sandbox lets commands reach only the hosts you allowed, and the Leon server is not one of them. Allowing its host does not help: the sandbox lets the network out only through a proxy, which Leon’s Node does not use. The hooks run outside the sandbox, so only the agent’s reads fail. A chained command stays inside the sandbox anyway: |, ;, &&, cd … &&, $( ), a backtick, a subshell, or any redirection except 2>&1. To check: grep -n leon/bin/leon ~/.claude/settings.json must show Leon’s read commands under sandbox.excludedCommands, and ~/.leon under sandbox.filesystem.denyWrite. What to do: with the passage usage, run ~/.leon/bin/leon setup in a terminal and answer y to “Let Leon's read commands run outside the Claude Code sandbox …? [y/N]”. A no is kept and not asked again: to change it, run ~/.leon/bin/leon retirer-crochets --usage passage, then ~/.leon/bin/leon setup. Without passage, or with a sandbox turned on elsewhere than in your user settings, add the exceptions yourself, in the settings where the sandbox is on. Under sandbox.excludedCommands, ten entries: ~/.leon/bin/leon and its absolute path (such as /Users/you/.leon/bin/leon), each followed by thread, thread *, threads, threads * and search *. And always ~/.leon under sandbox.filesystem.denyWrite: otherwise a sandboxed command could rewrite the launcher or the CLI, then have them run outside the sandbox through an exempted read. Never add them when ~/.leon/bin/leon runs a clone (the clone form, leon setup --depot): a sandboxed agent can change the code of the clone, and would run it outside the sandbox. That is why nothing is offered for the clone form. The agent must run the read alone: ~/.leon/bin/leon thread, or ~/.leon/bin/leon search followed by a few words.

permissionPrompts.title: Claude Code asks before every read
permissionPrompts.text: You see: Claude Code asks for your permission each time the agent runs ~/.leon/bin/leon thread or leon search, or the read is refused. Why: it is a Bash command like any other, under your permission settings. Leon never writes a permission rule. A permission decides whether Claude Code asks you; the sandbox decides whether the network gets through. To check: /permissions in Claude Code lists the active rules. What to do: if you want, add these rules to permissions.allow in your settings: Bash(~/.leon/bin/leon thread), Bash(~/.leon/bin/leon thread *), Bash(~/.leon/bin/leon threads), Bash(~/.leon/bin/leon threads *) and Bash(~/.leon/bin/leon search *). A command chained with another one is asked again. Under a sandbox, add its exception too (see “Reads fail inside the Claude Code sandbox”).

readUsage.title: A read command exits with code 1
readUsage.text: You see: a message that does not start with “Leon:”, and exit code 1. For example “leon threads takes no argument.”, “leon thread takes one id.”, “leon thread: the id must be the id of a thread (a uuid, as leon threads prints it).”, “leon search needs a query: …”, “leon search: this request is too long.” or “Unknown option '-d'. …”. Why: a usage error. There is an argument too many, a malformed id, a request too long for the server, or a word that starts with a dash, which Node reads as an option. Only usage errors exit with 1. To check: compare the command with the forms below. What to do: use ~/.leon/bin/leon threads, ~/.leon/bin/leon thread with or without an id, ~/.leon/bin/leon search followed by a few words, ~/.leon/bin/leon versions followed by an id (with --read and a number to print one version), and ~/.leon/bin/leon lessons. For search, give plain words, without apostrophes, backticks, $( ), ; or |: the shell could cut or run them. For a word that starts with a dash, put the words after --.

noteRefused.title: leon note saves nothing
noteRefused.text: You see: “Leon: … has not accepted writing notes to Leon from this computer (the noter consent): nothing was sent. …”, “Leon: the Leon server refused the note (the noter consent of this tool is missing): nothing was saved.”, “Leon: note not saved: its last version is not the one given with --version, it was written by another tool, or it does not exist. …”, “leon note needs --tool …” or “leon note: this note is too long.” Why: the noter usage is missing for the tool named by --tool. Or someone wrote a newer version first, or the note comes from another tool. Or the request is too heavy for the server. A note over 4,000 characters is cut without a word: “too long” comes only from a text full of control characters, which take up to 6 bytes each once escaped. To check: --tool must name the tool of the session: claude_code, codex, cursor or antigravity. What to do: run ~/.leon/bin/leon setup in a terminal to accept noter. For a version conflict, read the last version with ~/.leon/bin/leon versions followed by the id of the note, then write again with that number. Shorten a note that is too long.

emptyAnswers.title: “No thread found.” or “No results.”
emptyAnswers.text: You see: “No thread found.”, “No results.”, “No threads on this project yet.” or “No lessons for this project yet.” Why: these are normal answers, not failures. leon thread without an id reads the thread of the current branch, and a new branch has none yet. A thread or a source you cannot see (another person’s, or one whose usage was withdrawn) gets the same answer as one that does not exist. leon search searches only the current repository. To check: run the command from the folder of the right repository, connected with the right account (see “Sessions go to another account or workspace”). What to do: list the threads with ~/.leon/bin/leon threads, then read one with ~/.leon/bin/leon thread followed by its id.

externalSessions.title: “session externe : tâches et récit non repris” (external session: tasks and story not kept)
externalSessions.text: You see: in the start block, sessions marked “session externe : tâches et récit non repris”. Their threads stay poor, and leon thread gives little more than branches, pull requests and commits. Why: a session is external as soon as text from elsewhere came into it. That is the case with web tools (WebFetch, WebSearch), any MCP tool except Leon’s own local tools, the Workflow tool, any tool Leon does not know, and network commands in Bash (curl, wget, ssh, git clone, most gh commands). A subagent is judged the same way, and one whose exchanges are missing counts as external. Today the own tools of the Claude Code desktop app count too, so most of its sessions are external. Once external, a session stays external. Leon then keeps only its keys, so that text it cannot vouch for does not shape your memory. To check: look in the session for one of those tools or commands. What to do: nothing to repair. To feed the memory, do network work in another session. Declare Leon’s MCP server under the name leon, so that its local tools do not count (see “Reading Leon from a session”). Search still finds external sessions: ~/.leon/bin/leon search followed by a few words.

noSummary.title: A session has no summary
noSummary.text: You see: a session has no summary, although you accepted the resume usage. Why: a summary is written only for a session with at least 6 messages typed by you. Messages the tool adds in your place, tool results and the turns of a claude -p script do not count. It is written about a minute after a real end of session, or once 15 minutes pass without a new turn. A Claude Code session sends what the summary needs only at its end, or with an import: while it is open, it has no summary. A summary that waits more than an hour after the last sending (a busy queue, a stopped server, retries) waits for the next sending of that session. The model may also find nothing worth keeping. With no model on the server, no summary is ever written (see “No morning briefing”). To check: ~/.leon/bin/leon thread followed by the thread’s id shows no summary for that session. What to do: wait, or go on with the session. Check the usage with ~/.leon/bin/leon setup. For a short session, keep the essential with leon note.

noModel.title: No morning briefing
noModel.text: You see: “No briefing for this project yet: it will be ready at your next session.” or “The morning briefing is not prepared: no model is configured on this server.” Why: in the first case, the briefing is being prepared. In the second, the server has no model: it prepares no briefing, no summary and no written thread state. Reading, search and capture still work. To check: the text itself tells which case it is. What to do: in the first case, wait for your next session. In the second, ask the person who runs your Leon server to configure a model.

threadState.title: A thread shows lists but no written state
threadState.text: You see: leon thread shows the branches, pull requests and files of a thread, but no state written by the model. Or the written states disappear after leon retirer-crochets. Why: a written state is shown only if you can see all its sources, and only if their sessions keep the resume usage. Otherwise Leon shows the lists only, never an older written version. leon retirer-crochets withdraws the usages of the sessions already sent, so their written states fall back to lists. With no model on the server, no state is written at all. To check: ~/.leon/bin/leon setup offers resume if it is missing. What to do: give the usage again with ~/.leon/bin/leon setup: the state is written again in the background. To turn off only the read-first stop, use ~/.leon/bin/leon retirer-crochets --usage passage, not the full removal.

threadMissing.title: A session is in no thread, or a thread is missing
threadMissing.text: You see: leon thread without an id gives nothing useful, a session is in no thread, or a thread you expect is missing from leon threads. Why: a session joins the thread of its branch, or else of one of its pull requests. main and master never have a thread. Without a branch or a pull request, a session joins the closest thread through its summary, so without a summary it stays outside any thread. Two of your threads with the same branch or pull request merge into the oldest one: nothing is deleted. To check: git branch --show-current, and ~/.leon/bin/leon threads. What to do: work on a named branch, or open a pull request. Read the oldest thread that has the branch or the pull request.

projectKey.title: The project is split in two, or its name starts with dossier:
projectKey.text: You see: the threads of a repository do not show in another clone or on another computer, or the project is named dossier: followed by 16 characters. Why: the project key is github.com/owner/repository, read from the origin remote when it points to GitHub. Without such a remote (GitLab, a remote with another name, a remote through an SSH host alias such as git@github-work:… instead of github.com, no remote, a folder outside Git), the key comes from the absolute path of the folder where the session started, so a subfolder gives another project too. Another path, or another computer, then gives another project. A deleted worktree under the .claude/worktrees folder of a clone takes the key of that clone. To check: git remote get-url origin must give a github.com address. What to do: add or fix the origin remote, with github.com as its host, and open your sessions at the root of the repository. Then run ~/.leon/bin/leon import-claude-code with --project followed by the folder: sessions already sent get the new key.

searchMisses.title: leon search misses something you know is there
searchMisses.text: You see: leon search answers “No results.” or misses something you know Leon has. Why: it searches only the current repository: its sessions and its GitHub sources. Notes saved with leon note are not in that search today. Tool calls come only when the query asks for them. Without an embeddings provider on the server, search uses the words only, and new texts get their vectors a little later. To check: run it from the folder of the right repository (see “The project is split in two, or its name starts with dossier:”). What to do: search with other plain words. Read a known note with ~/.leon/bin/leon versions followed by its id, or find it with the search of the website. For tool calls, ask for them in the query: ~/.leon/bin/leon help shows how.

cutOrMasked.title: A text is cut, or a secret is masked
cutOrMasked.text: You see: a long message ends with “[…tronqué]” (“truncated”), a secret shows as “[secret masqué]” (“secret masked”), or the start block ends early. Why: each turn is kept up to 20,000 characters, then cut. The secrets Leon recognizes are masked before sending: they are neither stored nor searchable. The start block stays under 8,000 bytes, so the end of a long list of threads can be missing. To check: the mark is in the text itself. What to do: nothing: the cut part is not kept. Read a full thread with ~/.leon/bin/leon thread followed by its id. To keep the essential of a long passage, write a note with leon note. To find a masked secret, search for the words around it.

noReasoning.title: The reasoning of the agent is missing
noReasoning.text: You see: with the coulisses usage, the reasoning of the agent is still not in the thread. Why: Leon sends only what the tool writes in its transcript. With its default settings, Claude Code writes no reasoning text; with showThinkingSummaries on, it writes a summary in interactive sessions. Codex writes a summary, often empty. Cursor writes none, which is why coulisses is never offered for it. Antigravity writes it in full. To check: look for showThinkingSummaries in your Claude Code settings. What to do: turn on showThinkingSummaries in Claude Code if you want the summary. For the other tools, nothing can be done.

notYet.title: A session you just finished is not there yet
notYet.text: You see: a session you just finished is not yet in the search, or has no summary or thread. Why: everything after the sending runs in the background: indexing, filing into threads, the summary (see “A session has no summary”), the thread state and the vectors. To check: a few minutes later, search for a word of the session with ~/.leon/bin/leon search. What to do: wait. If nothing comes after several minutes, check that the session was sent (see “A Claude Code session did not arrive”). The person who runs the server can check that its workers run.

githubNotRead.title: Nothing new comes from GitHub
githubNotRead.text: You see: the morning briefing and the threads get nothing new from GitHub. Why: Leon reads only the team repositories that are checked. With none checked, GitHub is not read at all, whatever the connection. To check: in Settings › Workspace › Team repositories, a banner shows while nothing is checked. What to do: an owner or an admin checks the repositories there. They must be able to read each repository on GitHub themselves.

codexApprove.title: Codex: nothing arrives after the install
codexApprove.text: You see: Codex gets no block and no reminder, and nothing is captured. leon setup wrote “Codex runs a new hook only once you approve it: at the next start of Codex, type /hooks and approve the Leon hooks (in the Codex app: Settings › Hooks). …” Why: Codex runs a hook only once it is approved. A hook added later, such as the one of the reminder, must be approved too, and so must a hook whose command or options change. A Leon update that keeps the command asks for nothing. To check: /hooks in Codex shows Leon’s hooks as approved. grep -n crochet ~/.codex/hooks.json lists those Leon put there. What to do: at the next start of Codex, type /hooks and approve them. Do not edit their command in hooks.json. If Leon warns that config.toml also has [[hooks.*]] tables, Codex runs those too: keep Leon’s hooks in one place.

codexLate.title: Codex: a session arrives late (after /quit or codex exec)
codexLate.text: You see: a Codex session does not show up in Leon right away. Why: Codex does not run its end hook after /quit (the session stays alive in its background process). It does not run its turn hook in codex exec. To check: run ~/.leon/bin/leon rattraper: it counts the sessions it caught up. A file left in ~/.leon/entrees is something else: a session end whose hook was interrupted. What to do: nothing: the catch-up sends the session at the next start of a Leon hook, in any tool, or when you run that command.

cursorSilent.title: Nothing from Leon in Cursor, or in claude started in Cursor’s terminal
cursorSilent.text: You see: in Cursor, nothing from Leon (no block at the first message, nothing captured), although Cursor runs Leon’s Claude Code hooks. Or claude started in Cursor’s built-in terminal gets no block, no reminder and no stop, and its session is not captured. Why: Cursor runs Claude Code’s hooks too. Leon recognizes Cursor and keeps its Claude Code commands silent there on purpose, so that the block does not arrive twice. Cursor gets its block and its capture from its own hooks, in ~/.cursor/hooks.json. A claude started in Cursor’s terminal inherits CURSOR_VERSION, so all of Leon’s hooks stay silent there too. To check: grep -n crochet ~/.cursor/hooks.json must show crochet cursor prompt and crochet cursor tour. echo $CURSOR_VERSION must print nothing in the terminal where you start claude. What to do: set up Cursor’s hooks with ~/.leon/bin/leon setup (it offers Cursor when ~/.cursor exists). Start claude from a terminal outside Cursor. Send the missed Claude Code sessions with ~/.leon/bin/leon import-claude-code --project followed by the folder (see “A Claude Code session did not arrive”).

cursorHooks.title: Cursor: the hooks fail, or the block comes late
cursorHooks.text: You see: Cursor’s Leon hooks fail at launch (an EPERM error) or do not run. The installer warned “Warning: the launcher runs Leon from a clone in ~/Documents (…), a folder macOS does not let Cursor run scripts from: its hooks would fail. …” Or the block arrives only with your first message. Or a conversation opened with no folder never reaches Leon. Why: macOS does not let Cursor run a script stored in Documents, Desktop or Downloads; this hits only the clone form. Cursor does not wait for its start hook, so Leon sends the block with your first message, once per conversation. Cursor reads its hooks file by itself, but not always right away. A conversation with no folder (“No Repo”) is stored where Leon does not read. To check: ~/.cursor/hooks.json holds Leon’s entries. What to do: use the installed form (~/.leon/bin/leon setup without --depot), or move the clone out of those folders. Restart Cursor if its hooks do not run (“Cursor reads its hooks file on its own; if the Leon hooks do not run, restart Cursor.”). Open a folder before you start a conversation.

cursorLimits.title: Cursor: subagents and reasoning are missing
cursorLimits.text: You see: in a Cursor session, a subagent leaves nothing in the thread, the session stays external, and no reasoning shows. Why: Cursor’s transcript writes neither the result of a tool call nor the reasoning. In the Agents window, a subagent’s file holds a single error line (seen on a free account). So Leon cannot judge the subagent, and the session counts as external. To check: the session is marked “session externe : tâches et récit non repris” (“external session”) in the start block. What to do: nothing on Leon’s side. That is also why coulisses is never offered for Cursor.

antigravity.title: Antigravity: the block comes at the first message, or nothing runs
antigravity.text: You see: in Antigravity, the block arrives only at the first message, not when the conversation opens. Nothing happens right after the install. There is no reminder in an old version, nor in a conversation with no folder open. A command that failed shows the status ok in the thread. Why: the Antigravity app (2.0.1, tried) never calls its start event, so Leon sends the block before the first model call, once per conversation. Antigravity reads ~/.gemini/config/hooks.json only when it starts. The reminder needs your message in the hook’s input, which the app gives from 2.0.6 on, and an open folder. The app does not write the exit code of a command. A hooks.json with comments is never rewritten. And macOS does not let Antigravity run a script stored in Documents, Desktop or Downloads: with a clone stored there (the clone form), its hooks fail at launch with an EPERM error, and the installer warns “Warning: the launcher runs Leon from a clone in ~/Documents (…), a folder macOS does not let Antigravity run scripts from: its hooks would fail. …”. To check: grep -n leon ~/.gemini/config/hooks.json must show the leon entry, with crochet antigravity prompt and crochet antigravity tour. What to do: restart the app, the IDE or agy (“Antigravity reads this file when it starts: restart the app, the IDE or agy for the Leon hooks to run.”). Update the app for the reminder. Open a folder in the conversation. Remove comments from hooks.json, then run ~/.leon/bin/leon setup again. For the EPERM error, use the installed form (~/.leon/bin/leon setup without --depot), or move the clone out of those folders. Open Antigravity once before leon setup: ~/.gemini alone, the folder of Gemini CLI, is not enough. If leon setup says an earlier setup left Antigravity’s hooks in place, remove them with ~/.leon/bin/leon retirer-crochets --outil antigravity.

lecture.title: Reading Leon (usage "lecture", asked separately):
lecture.p1: At the start of each session or conversation, Leon places in the agent's context the summary of your work threads on this repository (keys only: their id, branch, tools, dates, pull request numbers and states, number of linked sources), which replaces the list of your recent sessions, the lessons you accepted, and an instruction to read the thread of its task. The model provider of the tool sees them. For this, the start request also sends the Leon server the usages this tool accepted and the Leon command of this computer (such as ~/.leon/bin/leon), which the instruction cites.
lecture.p2: The agent can read your work threads on this repository, their summaries and their state, the lessons you accepted, and the memory of this repository that you can see, with the commands leon threads, leon thread, leon search, leon versions and leon lessons, or with the tools threads, thread, versions and lessons if the Leon MCP server is connected to the tool. The model provider of the tool sees what it reads. This usage never lets an agent write anything to Leon.
lecture.p3: The leon commands use the token of this computer: once one of your code tools accepts this usage, they work for every agent on this computer. Refusing it in a tool only removes, in that tool, the summary, the lessons and the instruction placed at the start.

rappel.title: Reminder at each message (usage "rappel", asked separately):
rappel.p1: Each time you send a message, the hook sends the first 2,000 characters of your message (secrets masked before sending, and again by the server) only to the Leon server this computer is connected to, with the project key, the current Git branch, the session id, the name of the tool and the usages this tool accepted. The server neither stores nor logs your message: it only looks for those of your work threads on this repository that it touches.
rappel.p2: When it touches one or two of your threads not yet cited in this session, the server sends back one line of keys (their id, branch, tools, dates, pull request numbers and states, number of linked sources), which the tool adds to the agent's context: the model provider of the tool sees it. Otherwise nothing is added. The hook waits 1.5 seconds at most: without an answer by then, your message goes on without it.
rappel.p3: To cite a thread only once per session, the server keeps the list of the threads already cited in each session (never the message) for 24 hours, then deletes it within the next hour.

noter.title: Agent notes (usage "noter", asked separately):
noter.p1: The agent can keep notes in Leon with the command leon note. Each note sends the Leon server this computer is connected to the text of the note (4,000 characters at most, secrets masked before sending, and again by the server), with the project key, the name of the tool, the session id and the usages this tool accepted. The note can be read like your sessions (by you and, on the Leon website, by the managers above you) and keeps its versions: Leon's search finds it, and it is never placed as it is in the context of a session.
noter.p2: At the start of each session or conversation, the start request also sends the Leon server the usages this tool accepted, the Leon command of this computer (such as ~/.leon/bin/leon) and the name of the tool, and Leon places in the agent's context one sentence that gives this command to write a note, with the tool and the session id filled in (the session id only when it is safe in a shell). The model provider of the tool sees it.
noter.p3: Refusing it in a tool removes that sentence there, and leon note then sends nothing for that tool. It also turns off remember, the note tool of the Leon MCP server, for all your assistants connected to this Leon workspace, until you turn it back on in the Memory section of the Leon website settings.

claudeCode.withClaudeLead: Copy the instructions and paste them into Claude Code. It does the setup with you and tells you when to click “Authorize”. The boxes on that page are yours: it never ticks them or clicks for you.
claudeCode.instructions:
Install Leon on this computer and connect it to my coding tools.
1. Run this command in the terminal: {command}
If your sandbox blocks writing to ~/.leon or downloading from nodejs.org, ask me for permission to run it outside the sandbox.
2. If the script ends with “No terminal is available to ask you questions” and prints a last command that ends with “setup --url” followed by Leon's address: before you run it with the --yes option, copy to me, as is and without summarizing it, the text of what Leon will send (it is the “What is sent” section of {docs}) and wait for my explicit agreement. Never run --yes without my explicit agreement. If the script asks you questions instead of saying “No terminal is available…”, answer them with me.
3. Before you run that command, warn me that it opens my browser and waits for my click on “Authorize”, up to 5 minutes. Run it with a timeout of at least 5 minutes (your tool stops at 2 minutes by default) or in the background. The authorization page asks me to cancel if I did not run the command: remind me that you ran it for me. The page may also show boxes for usages (such as reading Leon), checked by default: they are mine. Never tick, untick or click anything on that page, and never open its address in a browser you control: only give it to me. If this computer is already connected, the command may open that page again for these boxes, and then waits about 100 seconds. If your sandbox stops it from opening the browser or listening on 127.0.0.1, ask me for permission to run it outside the sandbox. If the browser does not open, it prints the address to open: give it to me.
4. At the end, tell me which coding tools are connected and which Leon account this computer is connected to.
Never ask me for a token, read one or show one: the connection is made through the browser.
